utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. Vanderpuye has concluded the examination-in-chief. Now it's the turn of Mr. Tolimir to commence his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I extend my greetings to everybody present, and I wish that today's trial finish as God wishes and not as I wish. And I wish everybody a pleasant stay amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I only have some questions based on yesterday's examination-in-chief. Yesterday the witness when she was asked about the data given by Mr. Ivanisevic replied that she didn't pay much attention to that data because she does not hold Mr. Ivanisevic in high esteem. Is that the position of the OTP as a whole or your personal attitude?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify that what I said yesterday about Mr. Ivanisevic was different. I said that he -- first of all, I did pay a lot of attention to the list of 58 names provided on the basis of his book. Moreover, I already made some analysis of this list and provided the Court yesterday with preliminary results of my analysis. Secondly, I commented on the reliability of this source. I just said that I have my doubts regarding the reliability as Mr. Ivanisevic might be a biased source; this is what I said. And this is, of course, my personal opinion, and I wasn't speaking in the name of the OTP. So whatever is the opinion of the OTP, that the Prosecutor's Office should be expressing it separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying. So this is your personal opinion. If that is so, I would like to know why you are not so prejudiced or why don't you have the same attitude toward the investigation team of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their independent commission, whom you mentioned yesterday, and the president of that commission? Or perhaps you co-operated with them and therefore trust them more.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like that you specify what commission you have in mind. I can guess you referred to the commission for tracing missing persons, federal commission, but I don't think I mentioned this particular commission yesterday, so please clarify first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned Tokacevo [phoen]; do you remember? What is his position? You mentioned him and gave some assessments and therefore I would like you to explain why or based on what you form your attitude toward certain persons.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned, indeed, Mr. Tokaca, but he doesn't represent a commission. He's the head of a human rights NGO, and the NGO is called Research and Documentation Centre. I mentioned Mr. Tokaca and the Bosnian Book of Dead, this is the source on war victims, largest existing, that was compiled by this group of people, but as a matter of fact I was explaining why I was not using this source in my work. One of the reasons I gave was that this database is not the product of a professional statistical group; it is people who do work on improving the human rights situation in the country. And, well, I -- whenever I can, I avoid using these kind of sources in my work because there might be various biases in the information they provide. So being positive about the outcome of the work of Mr. Tokaca and the Research and Documentation Centre, generally, as an important contribution to the reconciliation process in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the same time I never used this particular data as a source for compiling a list of victims for the trials of this Tribunal. Well, that's all I can say. And I have the same attitude towards Mr. Ivanisevic. I consider this person as an activist involved in human rights area. And when using these kind of sources, one has to be extremely careful. First of all, it is necessary to realise these sources are not made by professional statisticians or demographers. Secondly, these sources have hidden biases. Often these sources rely on informants that are not checked and not confirmed to be reliable. So that's all I am saying. And from this point of view, my attitude towards Mr. Ivanisevic and anybody else is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take that position as a demographer based on the data given by Mr. Ivanisevic or based on his personal characteristics?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- first of all, I don't know Mr. Ivanisevic so I don't know his personal characteristics. I know things about him and I -- that's all I know about him. Second, the data, I just received a list of 58 names that I was unable to fully study yet as the information included in his book is extremely limited. It is too limited for me to make a reliable study of the reliability of this information. On the other hand, I am aware of cases where victims addressed by Mr. Ivanisevic were miscommunicated to the audience, outside audiences. For instance, I am aware of cases in Sarajevo that he reported victims as victims of the siege and as a matter of fact the families of these victims claimed the victims died natural deaths. So this is one example I can mention. So these kind of inconsistencies happen, simply. And I will present my clear opinion on this list and the 58 names at the time my analysis will be finished. Perhaps I should add that an RFA has been sent to the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to provide the OTP with complete documentation related to the 58 names. That simply means that the court decisions to which Mr. Ivanisevic referred in his book, I hope, can be collected and studied, and this will be very helpful. And only then I can give my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday that you checked the data provided by him in the log-books of died persons of Republika Srpska, so tell us why you checked on the data regarding died Muslims who died in Tuzla in the relevant registers in the Republika Srpska? Can you explain that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday I was searching for the 58 names in two databases, among others. The two databases included both, the RS Mortality Database and also Federal Institute of Statistics Mortality Database. So my search was complete and wasn't related to one of these databases only. So -- and the conclusion of this search was that I didn't find what -- this what I was looking for. Namely, I was expecting that in these two databases that are established based on documentation of death cases, either death certificates or other documents, the other documents would include court declarations, among others, so in this kind of databases that are complete to the extent they can be complete in the war time, I didn't see these records. So that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, if you checked, whether there are death certificates issued for these persons at the same time that was mentioned by Mr. Ivanisevic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Death certificates, I don't know whether they were issued or not. When I was searching through the databases, RS Mortality Database and FIS Mortality Database, as a matter of fact to check whether there were any records, entries, made by statistical authority based on the court declarations used by Mr. Ivanisevic, but, as I'm saying, I didn't find them, so I couldn't check whether any document confirming death was entered into the statistical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But yesterday you said during the examination on page 71 - the page reference may have changed - in line 19: I did not use Bosnian death registers from April 1992 through April 1995. Does that mean that in this case you did not check the data provided by Mr. Ivanisevic?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't recall this particular sentence, that I would have said something like that, and particularly that here you provided me with no context of this statement. So I would be -- I would feel much more comfortable if you first of all make a clear reference to the transcript and I can see it and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the Registry to put that part on the screen, if that is possible. Yes, they are working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you. I understand that it's page 11421.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, you were referring to line 19. Is that the part you want to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably line 19 or possibly 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It said, "I did not use Bosnian death registers from April 1992 through April 1995," and so on. And after that the witness mentioned Tokaca the -- or Mr. Tokaca's missing persons centre. I don't know, maybe my Legal Assistant and I will be able to give an exact reference to the witness after the break, but she said that she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just wait a moment. The Registry is working on it, and I think we will have it on the screen immediately. Not sure if this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, can you help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that this is the correct page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have the part on the screen you are referring to, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the clarity of the record, this is page 11422, lines 19 and 20. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked the witness whether that means that she did not check the list of 58 persons given by Ivanisevic against the death registers at all, and when she said that she did not use this so-called Bosnian book of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the source of confusion, my confusion, was the term "death register." The death register is the RS Mortality Database and FIS Mortality Database which I have used to search for the 58 records. Mr. Tolimir, however, used the term "death register" in the context of the Bosnian Book of Dead, which is the database of Mirsad Tokaca's Research and Documentation Centre. It is an NGO database, not a death register as the RS and FIS Mortality Databases. It's an important difference because the death register is a official source or official archive where all death records in a country are kept. These are the death registers of the federal authorities, statistical authority, or RS statistical authority. And I did search through these registers. The Tokaca's database is not a death register; it is an NGO list of victims. A list that is based on all kinds of sources. But unfortunately, Tokaca has no access to official documents confirming the death of people, like death certificates, court declarations, any other documentation. He compiled this database on sources like informants' statements, published lists of victims, ICRC records of missing persons, other records of missing persons. Even they studied cemeteries and were collecting names of victims from the grave stones. It's a totally completely different type of source. And the reliability of the BBD must be seen differently compared with the official death registers. So once again, I did search in the official death registers, both RS and the federal. I didn't search in the Bosnian Book of Dead because there was no point in searching in the Bosnian Book of Dead. It is not a death register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a point of clarification. The witness referred to the FIS Mortality Database, which isn't recorded correctly in the transcript. It should be FIS. It refers to the Federal Institute for Statistics in Sarajevo, and the correction should be made to pages -- page 5, line 22, and then again at page 8, lines 1 and line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be corrected for sure. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have enough time to waste on this, but I would like to take a look at page 11421, lines 18 and the following, where the witness says that she received the database from the statistical bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska and so on. And later on she says: I need excerpts from death registers and we didn't make lists of died persons in 1995. We did have lists of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question is, what is more relevant: The list of missing persons compiled by international organisations, or NGOs, or death registers issued by official bodies for the needs of citizens to exercise their rights based on these certificates? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is regarding what you said about what I said; I don't want to comment on this but not all was correct. I want to answer the question. Here is the thing, when there is no war, the information from the death register is crucial, of course, and official and is used by citizens for all kinds of purposes, including acquiring property rights and other purposes. During the war, statistical system is not working properly, so obviously the death registers are incomplete and often miss large numbers of deaths that occurred during the war. But there is one particular group of people who are not included in the death register. These are the missing persons. The persons missing cannot be included in the death registers for obvious reasons. There are no death certificates, certificates, as their bodies of the missing persons are in an unknown place and remain not available, so there is no way that a missing person can be registered by statistical authority. So there must be, when counting victims of war, their activities must go using many channels. It is not that we can rely on the death registers only, because this is not the way to do it. From the death registers the known deaths can be taken. However, missing persons must be looked for in other sources. The major source for reporting of missing persons is the International Committee for Red Cross. They have been doing this for a very, very long period of time and were involved in very many conflicts in the world. So they are the first one to go to affected areas and take reports from the families about their loved ones. ICRC collects information about detained persons, often visits the detention camps, checking on the condition of detention, but parallel, they also register the persons missing. So international organisations like ICRC is an important source for this kind of information. Whether the NGOs lists are an important source, yes, they are. Most definitely they are. But while ICRC have been working with established procedures, they have, for instance, a standardised questionnaire that is used to register missing persons. They are very selective when accepting reports on the missing. For instance, not anybody can come and report and the record will be made. Only family members, close family members, are accepted as informants to the ICRC. So these are these procedures that make the record of information on the missing persons very reliable. NGOs don't work in this way. In most cases they operate in post-conflict situations and they don't have these established standard practice to collect this data. So they usually accept any report from anybody, also all kinds of books, local reports are accepted, which is not always a good thing to do. So while working with the NGO lists one has to be much more careful and selective and critical while looking at this data and accepting this data. So it is just a matter of an approach that is needed while taking data from all these sources. And I believe the demographers here at the ICTY have been aware of these kind of problems and we have been careful and selective while choosing our sources. So perhaps I will finish here; it's too long. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Please tell us this: Why do you look for what you have and not what was indicated to you? For example, Mr. Ivanisevic puts forth a list of missing persons who may not have been registered though, but that person must have had a death certificate issued to the family either before the war or after the war, so why didn't you go and look for that? So is it up to him to point out the discrepancies in the lists you relied the most on?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, first of all, Mr. Ivanisevic didn't present us with death certificates for the 58 persons. He presented us with court declarations which are based on witness statements, and usually it is enough to present the court with two witnesses and based on what they say, the court would issue a declaration. So it is not a death certificate. A death certificate is a document that is issued by a medical profession, by a coroner in some cases, but generally by a physician who after examining the body describes the causes of death, and not only a single cause of death but three major causes of death, and puts his signature on the medical examination result. So I would like to stress, Mr. Ivanisevic did not provide death certificates. Your question, why didn't I look for death certificates, but I did. My answer is: But I did. It is not accidental that the two death registers, the RS death register and the FIS death register, are available in this office in my unit. These two databases actually didn't exist in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were made at the request that came from my unit and me personally, and we helped them to establish these databases by providing electronic tools to do so. We established the formats of databases in which they could computerise this information for us on the first place. So a lot of work has been done for this Tribunal in order to make it possible to have information about the official death notifications. And we do exactly know for whom a death certificate is available and for whom it isn't. So I did search in these databases. Unfortunately, in case of Srebrenica, these databases are not relevant because they cover known deaths which is a different, separate category from missing persons. The 2009 report that we submitted in this case is a report about missing persons, missing persons once again, and the missing persons is our initial group of victims or type of victims we take into consideration. In next step we proceed to other sources. Most importantly, we study the DNA-based identifications provided to us completely independently by an organisation different than the Red Cross. This different organisation is the ICMP, International Commission for Missing Persons, mandated to provide DNA identifications of persons exhumed from mass graves and other graves in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So my answer is: I did look for the death certificates and other official death notifications, but for Srebrenica project this is not the right source to use. It must be other sources, missing persons list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. I understand you. You have a need to say a lot, although it takes away a lot of our time. I'm asking you to follow the line of my questions and then try to indeed answer what I asked you. You will be given an opportunity to say what you want to say, but I wanted to address the issue of your approach to the documents and data provided by Mr. Ivanisevic. I will read from page 84 of yesterday's transcript. I don't know what page that is currently, but there you say: I compared that data with the database of the RS. That is line 11 of yesterday's page 84. Then you continue: This type of document which can be accepted based on the database of the RS makes me ask myself what kind of documents are those that Ivanisevic relied on. He is an activist. He may be biased towards the interest of the Serbian people. He supported Radovan Karadzic and co-operated with his Defence. He is not a statistician. Et cetera. If you had some access to pieces of information and if you approached it from the point of view of the person who provided it, how can we verify that? For example, why did you provide this description of his in order to denounce the data he put forth?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided the description of his in order to let the Chamber know that he might be biased and not reliable as a source. At the same time, I said yesterday, and I'm repeating today, I already studied these 58 names in order to provide the Chamber with a conclusion of these 58 cases, missing persons that should be taken off from the OTP list or not. That is what I'm doing and this is what I will be doing, disregarding what I think of the reliability of Mr. Ivanisevic and his sources. I think the most important thing is to give the Court the answer about these 58 names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, page 84, line 11, is now page 11435 of yesterday's transcript. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise for not having indicated the correct page immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mention Mr. Tokaca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were right. There's no reason for apology. The number has -- have just changed, and I wanted to assist you with the correct number. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you mentioned Mr. Tokaca and his, as called it today, the humanitarian NGO called the Centre for Documentation and Research. Since you assign a degree of importance to that organisation, did you receive a list of 500 people from him who turned out to be alive?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did receive a list, but not of 500 but 240 people. I am aware of the discussion in the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 500 potential survivors that Tokaca allegedly included in his database, the Bosnian Book of Dead. The OTP requested this list of 500 in order to be able to cross-reference this list with our sources, that would be the Srebrenica list of missing persons. In response we received a letter in which Tokaca says that he's unable to provide the list of 500 because the 500, be it 500 or approximately 500, whatever, his database, he explained, is made in such a way that any record deleted from the database at some point cannot be recovered anymore. So he clarified that in the course of time possibly the -- his centre have identified, they did, 500 survivors of Srebrenica who were immediately excluded from the records of the database. In order to provide us with what he had and what was still available, he sent us a list of 240 names. And these 240 names he said were coming -- first of all, are not in the records of war victims in his database, but they are aware of these names at this stage still and this is why they are providing this. So these 240 names were provided to us. Interestingly it was claimed that these 240 names were established based on ICTY sources and even more interestingly based on the Demographic Unit sources. Anyway, whatever the source for the 240 names, we did compare them with the Srebrenica list and drawn certain conclusions. May I talk further, Mr. Tolimir, or do I need to stop now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it would be interesting to hear for the Chamber when -- what you found out when checking out the 240 which did not make part of the original 500 group, if I understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood correctly. The 240 were cross-referenced with our list of missing and identified persons. One person of the 240 was confirmed in the DNA identification record of ICMP. One person. I think it was Mr. Ridic, as far as I remember his first name -- surname. We have run a small investigation because it is not possible that a person identified through DNA matching is alive at the same time. Importantly, the source we discovered, our source that this person could have been seen as a survivor, potential survivor, was a report on -- of this person in the government register of internally displaced persons and refugees. So he was in two sources. On one hand, DNA identification was available of his remains from a mass grave or other grave; on the other hand, there was a record of this person being reported at some point as a displaced person. The investigation clarified that the record in the register of internally displaced persons was not correct. Obviously the wife who, with two daughters, survived Srebrenica and ended in a territory controlled by the Government of Bosnia reported entire family as internally displaced persons. So he was registered as well, and he was registered in hope that at some point he will -- he would show up and rejoin the family. This never happened, and that was the reason that the record of him being an IDP was not correct. So the record of identification, of course, remains valid and confirms that the person did not survive Srebrenica. And the record of ICRC reporting him as a missing person and our record of including him as a Srebrenica missing person and subsequently as identified person is correct. All in all, there are no survivors from these 240 names that are included, at the same time at the OTP list, analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You now explained about one person. What about the other 239? Could that list be provided so that those names do not resurface yet again?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other 239 persons were not on the list of OTP, not on the missing persons list, not on the identified person list. So this is one, I think. Second, if you want, of course, you can have the list and you can run your searches, whatever you wish to do with the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was informed by my Legal Assistant that he does have the list. I want to put another question. What about the 500 mentioned by Mr. Tokaca, does he have a list of the 500?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he confirmed that these approximately 500 or another number of survivors were excluded from the records of war victims in his centre. However, he was unable to complete -- to provide us with the actual list of 500 names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to grasp what documents were used to introduce that data in his database? Do you have some sort of a basis that you could try to reconstruct the process? Otherwise all you can do is simply disregard what he said.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm not working with Mr. Tokaca and I -- why would I be interested in his sources? So it is -- yeah, what was possible, the 240, we checked and concluded there are no problems with survivors based on this list. But other than that I have no theories or nor sources for the 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be important for the OTP to have the list of 500 so that those names could not appear again as missing persons or persons whose names will be used in random samples so that no one could abuse the fact of the existence of those names? Was that figure perhaps put forth intentionally to focus the attention of those who are trying to do research about the missing persons in order to prove the existence of illogical occurrences on the list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Tokaca clarified about these 500, that it was partly a confusion created by the media around this number, magical number of 500, so I want to clarify this as well. Generally, however, I think that the issue of survivors of Srebrenica shouldn't be seen in the context of a single list of 500. If we think a little bit about how many people were located in Srebrenica by mid-1995 and how many of them were later registered as internally displaced persons, so we can say it is a large group. It is far larger than 500. And we have been working with the records of internally displaced persons in this particular project as well, so these would be the records from the government register, Bosnia-Herzegovina government register of internally displaced and refugees, that is a huge source. As of the year 2000, for the entire country, there was 580.000 people registered still, almost 600.000, of internally displaced, with a small group of refugees. We ourselves use as well, systematically, voters registers from 1997 election, from 1998 election, from 2000 election, so each of these register is approximately two point half million people for the entire country. The Srebrenica population is covered there. They are there. So -- and we've been cross-referencing the missing persons records with sources on post-war survivors. So survivors is absolutely not a list of 500. It is a much more complex and broader issue than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He stated that the 500 come from the total number of the Srebrenica victims. I'm asking you this: Does the number of 500 can be used later on with some researchers, like Ivanisevic, that the 58 were indeed on the list but had died before the war or after the war so that they could say that they had taken them off the list? We don't have the list of 500. It should be provided. It should not be made use of as a, say, reserve sample which can later be used for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, sir, you really should contact Mr. Tokaca about this and discuss this with him. Or perhaps Mr. Ivanisevic could do that, but that is all I can say. And I don't know exactly what Tokaca said to the press. It is not necessarily so that what the press wrote about it is exactly what he said to the press. These things happen. Miscommunication is a common thing in press reports in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify this matter, I would like to ask you to help me to understand it fully. You have contacted Mr. Tokaca and asked him about the sources and the background of these media reports of a 500-persons list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I requested the list, simply, of 500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you received a list of 240?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. But this is a different list, obviously, than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he said that he didn't keep the 500, eliminated in earlier years, from his records of war victims. He didn't keep copies of these records. They were just deleted. You know, this is what a real statistician would never do, but people who work for NGOs don't have this background and they do. They just delete. And that's it. They are lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tokaca tell you if these 240 people on the list provided to you were part of the 500?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't tell this. But I understood that this is a separate list. Which is, by the way, not part of his records on war victims, because these are potential survivors, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tokaca confirm that he was in the possession of such a list of 500 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't, as a matter of fact. He even clarified that it didn't have to be exactly 500. It was just a number he mentioned that came to his mind, right. But he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday you also mentioned a request you sent to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was page 79. You asked them to forward their list to be compared with yours. Mr. Vanderpuye asked you what it was that you asked them to change, and you answered - it was document 2770 on the 65 ter list: It is an RFA sent to the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it in e-court so that the witness could peruse it, and then I'll have a few questions of her. Thank you. It is P2083. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At page 14431 of yesterday's transcript, I think it was line 8 and before that at page 14430, you mentioned the need to verify the 142 names and what you did at first. Then Mr. Vanderpuye asked you this: You sent documents to the Bosnian authorities asking that they check the document against dates of death. We wanted to receive information, and I don't know why we would ask them to change anything. Then you go on to say, We received entries, et cetera, et cetera. My question is this: Since this document has not been translated, can you tell us which paragraph we should read and what paragraph 3 has to do with so as to be able to know what kind of request was sent to the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you see on the screen the document, the request for assistance, in English and B/C/S. Yesterday the translation was not on the screen because it was put together in one document, and that was the reason we only marked it for identification pending translation. But this problem is now resolved. We have the document in both versions on the screen. And I think yesterday the Prosecution has tendered this document and now it will be admitted in full. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I only saw this translation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So could you tell us, did you receive documents from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the documents mentioned in paragraph 3 in the last sentence, which mentions evidence of these persons' death and the circumstances of their deaths or disappearances? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you make these documents available to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure the Defence has them already because it's impossible that they wouldn't be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I apologise. I was just informed by my assistant that it was indeed disclosed to the Defence but he didn't mark it as such. He simply gave the documents to me to study. So I apologise to everybody for this mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My following question: So you asked them to provide these documents, so why did you make the corrections and amendments so that they were detrimental to the information found and possessed by the army, I'm talking here about the Army of BiH, and not also to the other side?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I must clarify that we needed the documents to confirm or reject certain cases of military people included in our list of missing persons. So because of the discrepancies in the date of disappearance or death reported on one hand by ICRC and on the other hand in the army records, the documents in a large number of cases provided us with the confirmation that these are people who went missing in the fall of Srebrenica. So what was provided to us was the corrected, as I call it, corrected new date in the military records. But I didn't have to correct in anything in our records of ICRC because obviously the army records were consistent with the ICRC records. So it was just the justification -- the provided documents gave me the justification to keep these cases as the cases of missing persons and related to the fall of Srebrenica. That is all what was done in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you investigate and double-check the accuracy of those entries or whether they were fictitious in order to satisfy certain needs?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be kind of weird if I would have challenged the official documents sent to us by the authorities, state authorities, of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I didn't check the authenticity. I assume they were authentic, as I had no reason to assume they were fictitious. They were official documents provided to us in response to an official RFA, request for assistance, that is, yeah, a legal document, legally-binding document in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the Court's information and perhaps for the information to General Tolimir, the response to the RFA actually includes these documents that the witness is referring to. And the response was 65 ter 2771, P2084. And beginning on page 3 of that document you'll see the list of individuals and dates of death provided by the Bosnian authorities followed by a list of certificates. Just for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document was admitted into evidence yesterday. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you make any changes in the list that you provided and in the lists that were provided to you by this international organisation pursuant to your request?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. But generally speaking we don't change information in our original sources. When we make a list of Srebrenica missing, OTP list of Srebrenica missing, we use the reports of ICRC as -- exactly as they are reported. So we don't correct information provided by ICRC. The same is with the ICMP records of Srebrenica identified. We don't correct them unless, in case of ICMP, we corrected a few typos which we discussed with ICMP and clarified these typos. So it is not what we do. We don't correct. We cross-reference our lists with other sources, like military records. If there are inconsistencies, we clarify inconsistencies. And based on the clarification either we leave our records on the OTP lists as they are or we remove them. This is as simple as that. So it is a source, military records, any other additional list that we use in our work, like the census, RS Mortality Database, FIS Mortality Database, these are sources that help us in improving our understanding of every case, whether it is right to keep it on our list of OTP victims, Srebrenica victims, or not. That is how we work. And we don't change the original information from sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have a problem with your last question. I really don't understand it. We were talking about a request for assistance and an answer. And in your last question, page 24, lines 21 to 23, you are asking the witness about "the lists that were provided to you by this international organisation pursuant to your request." What do you mean by "this international organisation"? The request was addressed to the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is not an international organisation. And I think the answer was provided by this national institution. Was it -- did you misspoke or was it something else? I don't know. I would like to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's probably that my question was a bit illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on basis of what did you determine that the documents provide by the BiH army do not correspond to the lists provided by the OTP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I have to ask for a little clarification. Documents provided by the BiH army, I mean, you refer here -- you are referring here to the response to the RFA, I assume. And further, do not correspond to the list provided to the OTP; I assume here you refer to the military lists that we used to identify the inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I stop you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the record I see that Mr. Tolimir asked you that the BH army lists do not correspond to the lists provided "by the OTP" and not "to the OTP."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume it was "to the OTP." "By the OTP." I am confused. This is why I'm asking for more clarification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please clarify your question so that we can receive a reliable answer. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour - greetings to everybody - I think that this was a mistake in interpretation. Mr. Tolimir didn't speak about lists provided to or from the OTP. He was simply speaking about the OTP lists. So on one hand we have the BiH lists and on the other hand we have the OTP lists, for example the list dating from 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Are you now able to answer the question, or shall we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- ask Mr. Tolimir to rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I will say how I understand it, and perhaps Mr. Tolimir will say that it is right or not. So on one hand we have the 2009 OTP list of missing persons based on ICRC reporting, and then we have the RFA. And then we have the corrections, or new information, new documents, sent to us with regard to a number of cases. Is it correct this is what I am going to comment -- I'm supposed to comment on, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. You gave a correct answer. So the ICRC requested you to harmonise their lists with the lists from the BiH army; is that true? Was that the reason that you sent that request for assistance?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. ICRC has nothing to do with our request. It was our decision. At the time we saw there were inconsistencies in reporting of date of disappearance for a number of cases, 220 cases in total, when the ICRC reporting was compared to with the reporting in the military records that are here at the OTP at our disposal, so at that moment we decided to request additional information that would explain us the date of disappearance of death, place of disappearance of death, and any other circumstances for these inconsistent cases. At that time it was 142. 142 cases, not 220. Later new cases were added to this list. And we decided, without the ICRC, and requested clarification, documents were sent, we compared the response in the documents with the ICRC reporting and concluded for many cases we have no issue at all because the reporting became consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The ICRC report that you mentioned just now, did it contain the data about the manner of death, the date of death, and similar; or is it a list made solely on the basis of the reports of missing persons made by, say, parents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are reports of missing of certain individuals, with the date of going missing and place of going missing included in the informants' reports. But missing is, of course, not the same as reports on death. So reports on death are not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does death mean that the data on death and manner of death in the BiH list were changed; or were those data changed in the ICRC report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think BiH list, I understand that this is the response to the RFA, so I want to stress, nothing was changed in the ICRC reporting, with or without the response to the RFA. That is all I can say because I don't know what more you would like to hear about that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want anything more than this. It is now clear to me. I simply wanted to find out which list was changed based on this intervention from you, and now I concluded that the changes were made in the list by the BiH army. And this is enough for me. On page 11404, lines 16 to 19, you said: I worked as the Prosecution witness so that those reports contain the perspective of the OTP. Did I quote you correctly here, what you said at 14404? I'm talking about the transcript of the 16th of March, 2011, lines 16 to 19.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I probably said this in the context of my CV and my testimonies that I completed so far. I didn't mean -- well, it's a fact that I have been the Prosecution witness, expert witness. In one case I was called as a Defence witness, in Lukic and Lukic case. And I also acted as a Chambers witness, that would be the Khmer Rouge Tribunal in Cambodia. I was called by the investigative judges and not by any of the parties, not by the Prosecution, not by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have to check the page number. The transcript of yesterday ends with the last page 11436. There is no page 11404. Oh, no, I made a mistake. I correct myself. You are correct. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I wanted to address. The page is 11404, lines 23 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is correct. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Aleksandar. My notes are not entirely correct, and they are subjective.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does your report reflect the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the question to be repeated because the interpretation was somewhat shortened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was: Does your report reflect the views proposed by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects exclusively my views as a researcher and the author of this report, and I'm absolutely free in expressing the views that I can document and justify in a scientific way. And I'm not told by anybody what kind of views I should be expressing. My unit and I myself was never part of any trial team or investigative team. It has been always a separate unit, and we have always did our best to produce reports that would be unbiased and independent, and I hope we achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I base my question on what you said. It was you who said that your reports contained the perspective of the OTP. Please don't be angry at me. I quoted you verbatim.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did, but I think what you did not quote was the context of what I said. And the context was the testimonies and my acting as an expert witness. I just wanted to make it clear for which side I acted in these testimonies, most times, of course. Not exclusively. Most times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think rather than going around on this issue based on General Tolimir's recollection of what Dr. Tabeau said and her recollection of what she said, it might be best to put up in e-court on the screen what she actually said in this context. And that can be found at page 11404 through 11405 of the transcript. In particular, I think the quote that General Tolimir was relying on can be found at lines 22 through 25 and then into the next page. Beginning on page 11404.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will come up on the screen. There it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I see it on the screen as well? Can you help me this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 11404, line 22.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It seems to me that Mr. Vanderpuye want us to move to another topic, so let us do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just to be fair to both sides, Mr. Vanderpuye just wanted to put this part of yesterday's transcript on the screen. And there it is. You may continue in the way you wish. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I cannot continue because I don't understand the transcript, so I can only ask something related to yesterday's examination based on my own notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So when we are talking about 11404, line 4, he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, just a moment. We have now the wrong page on the screen. We wanted to have 11404, which was on the screen just before. There it is again. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Today you also stated that you were invited by the Tribunal to draft an expert report on Khmer Rouge. And Mr. Vanderpuye yesterday asked you about it. My question is: You were talking about a number of cases on which you worked, so were you ever engaged to work for a party that was not the victorious side in a particular war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just mentioned that I was called by the investigative judges of the Khmer Rouge Tribunal in Phnom Penh to work on a report which was definitely not associated with the Prosecution or the Defence. So I think this is a good example of working for the party who is completely -- who was completely independent and not involved in the conflict. Another time I was the witness for the Defence in Lukic and Lukic case. So does it answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, who was prosecuted in Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge or the people who vanquished them?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, cases in Khmer Rouge Tribunal are of those who are seen responsible for the mass scale victimisation in this period in that country. But you must be aware of the fact that it is not so that the highest rank politicians kill people, themselves, with their own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that. But since you did the research, I'm asking you, is there a single victim of the war in Cambodia that was killed by somebody else and not the Khmer Rouge? And I'm talking here about the victim that was contained in your relevant report.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is important to remember that in my reports I don't discuss the perpetrators. I don't say who killed whom and why. It is beyond this report, I think, that the work of a statistician and demographer is not the one that should be answering these kind of questions. So in the Khmer Rouge report that I made, also in this report, I didn't discuss the perpetrators and the people responsible for the mass killing. And, yeah, whether any victim was killed by a person not associated with the Khmer Rouge, I didn't discuss these kind of issues, simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it is a well known fact that one person stand trial in Phnom Penh. We must have our first break now and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to give a little correction to a question Mr. Tolimir asked me towards the end of the previous session, if you allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir asked me whether I worked for a party that was different than victors of war and I gave an answer which I'm not very happy with. I want to clarify that. I don't feel I work for parties to the conflict, to those who in the end had won or lost the war. My feeling is different. It is that I work to assist Trial Chambers in a better understanding of the victimisation of these wars. And this has nothing to do with parties to the war winning or losing; it is a different, completely different, thing and has nothing to do whether I work for the Prosecution or the Defence. It has always been that I was providing assistance to clarify certain issues and has nothing to do with parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Please tell us if your reports that you made for the Cambodia Tribunal and your report which you made in 2009 for this Tribunal are neutral with regard to the manner in which a person lost his or her life. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think generally the report is most definitely objective and independent. It is a report in which I make an assessment of the many existing estimates of the victims numbers of the Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia, and I take into account very different estimates provided by very different authors, some associated with the Khmer Rouge. And I don't make a problem of it. But whether it is neutral with the -- neutral with regard to the manner in which a person lost his or her life, I won't really understand what is the meaning of that. People died in Cambodia in all kinds of ways. Many of them died as indirect victims. Many were direct victims of this war. And I address these issues. I addressed that the indirect victims were a large group among all the victims. But I believe it is the only way to do it by just studying these two groups and showing the circumstances of life and death in the Khmer Rouge period in Cambodia. So my answer would be, yes, it is neutral with regard to the manner in which a person died. I wouldn't know what more Mr. Tolimir meant with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us not go as far as Cambodia. Let's go into the war into former Yugoslavia. As a demographer, did you engage in demographic studies of the expulsion of the Serb population affected by the war in Croatia or Bosnia, specifically Srebrenica or the Medak pocket and so on? Do your reports contain any information about any expelled or displaced Serb from any of the countries of former Yugoslavia? Is there -- to be more specific, is there a report on any killed Serb in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are very many questions in one question. Well, I will try to answer it, perhaps generally. Expulsions as such of Serb or any other ethnic group wasn't subject of my report. However, I did study the forced migration or generally, more generally, population -- war-related population migration, especially in the region of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In any report I made on this subject, and there is a high number of reports related to these issues, all ethnic groups were treated equally. There was no differentiation at our side to pay more attention to Serbs or Bosniaks or Croats. They were all treated in exactly same equal way. Another question was whether I studied the migration, war-related migration, of the Serb population from Croatia. I didn't make any report on this issue. Further, displaced Serbs from any of the countries of the former Yugoslavia, as I said, for Bosnia and Herzegovina we have reports that cover the entire country and all groups, that means including the Serbs. I didn't study this for Kosovo. Somebody else studied Kosovo. And regarding is there a report on any killed Serb or Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think that several reports include -- actually, all reports always included all ethnic groups. For instance, there is a group of Serb victim in Sarajevo reports most definitely. And in Srebrenica cases the fact that there are no Serb victims reported is not related to the fact that we have been selective and focused our attention exclusively on the Bosnian Muslims; it is what the data is telling us, that the victims of Srebrenica are almost exclusively the Bosnian Muslims and not Serbs. So it is what I'm trying to say, I always take unbiased equal approach with regard to all ethnic groups. And the results of every project depend on what really happened in certain war episodes. I am not a person who determines the outcomes of my analysis. They are as -- as -- they are just describing the reality of that time. Perhaps not perfectly, but to the extent it is possible they do describe the realities of certain war episodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I kindly ask you to focus on my questions. Do you know that the Muslims killed more than three and a half thousand Serbs in Srebrenica during this war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you are saying, sir, and I am not going to comment on it because I would need much more to comment than just your statement. If you provide me with a report which will be clear about sources and methods in which this number will be produced, then I can give you my assessment of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an employee of the OTP, did you investigate the Serb victims of the activities of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in the case of Naser Oric, so I didn't study.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your Demographic Unit work for the needs of the OTP and deal with this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We deal with projects that are addressed to us by various trial teams, so we work on Srebrenica because at some point this project was simply addressed to this unit. So in response several reports were made and submitted. It is not so that there are resources at the Office of the Prosecutor to involve in all kinds of issues. It is a matter of the needs of the Office and the needs that are addressed, are taken, and elaborated, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's not go into that any further. We discussed Srebrenica, and I said that victims -- there were victims on both sides. And you are answering that you only did what you were commissioned to do. But about the report that you submitted, you made it together with Mr. Bloomberg [as interpreted]. And what was the division of labour between the two of you, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may correct the name: It is Mr. Brunborg, not Bloomberg, as it says in the transcript. The division of work was the following: Mr. Brunborg is the author of the first Srebrenica report. He proposed the methodology and the sources that were used in the first Srebrenica report. I'm referring to the 2000 report of -- presented in the Krstic case. Mr. Brunborg at that time worked together with another young researcher, Henrik Urdal from Norway. Later, we got involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly first answer my question and then expand. Thank you. I asked about the report from 2009 which you made together with Mr. Brunborg, who was also an OTP witness as you are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All in all, Mr. Brunborg contributed at conceptual level and he also provided us with his comments on the work that was done in the Office of the Prosecutor. I worked on the report together with Mr. Arve Hetland [Realtime transcript read in error "Hedland"], who was responsible for preparing the databases and matching of records. I did all the analysis and wrote the report. Mr. Brunborg commented on all the steps of the preparation of the report. The name missing from the transcript is Arve Hetland. I said I worked on the report together with Mr. Arve Hetland. Instead of D it should be T. Hetland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These kind of things will be corrected later, at a later stage. You see this little sign there, that shows that that has to be checked with the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, please tell us, did you and Mr. Brunborg only carry out statistical analyses or demographic changes too? What did you do about these two things? Thank you. Actually, I mean the causes of demographic changes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report doesn't discuss the causes of the going missing and it is just about the measuring of the process itself. And eventually measuring as well, the identification reports on the initial missing persons reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, did you do that only based on the data you received from the OTP, or what were the other sources of information, if any? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: All sources used in the 2009 report were collected by my unit. So I didn't receive sources from other sections of the OTP. And I can repeat what I said yesterday about the sources that we used. So in brief it would be ICRC lists; ICMP records of identified persons, for the basic lists; for the integration of the missing persons lists with the identified, DNA identified persons. In addition to these we used the population census of 1991; several post-war sources on survivors; voters registers of 1997, of 1998, of 2000; BiH government registration of internally displaced persons and refugees. We also used, as a contextual source, the 1997 records of the so-called Srebrenica refugees. We used military records that were discussed earlier today. And I think that would be the major sources. Occasionally we might have contacted several other smaller sources, or consulted, not contacted, consulted several smaller sources, but the major sources are the ones I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 65 ter 1708 in e-court. That is D159. Thank you. Thank you. We are interested in page 4 in English and in Serbian -- or rather, in Serbian, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which reads, in the lower -- in the lower paragraph, it's in italics: "What was the minimum number of victims" -- or better -- let's start this way: Did you get any guide-lines as to what you should investigate, and, if so, were these guide-lines given to you by the OTP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't receive any guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what Mr. Brunborg said. I'm quoting now, bullet point 1: "What was the minimum number of victims from Srebrenica who were killed by the VRS after the fall of the enclave on July 11 1995 who can be identified by name?" Second bullet point: "What is the reliability of this list of victims?" Now, let us see, is the task of the Demographic Unit of the OTP correctly described in this passage? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This passage has nothing to do with my reports and the 2009 report in particular. It is an article that Helge Brunborg and Henrik Urdal had written together at some point, and it is just a separate thing. It is not part of the work done for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have the first page of this document on the screen so that we can familiarise ourselves with it. And I note that I don't find this document in the list of potential exhibits to be used during cross-examination of this witness. Now we see it's an article we have seen during the examination of Mr. Brunborg. Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As we see, he here speaks about accounting for it. So my question is: How do you and the Demographic Unit investigate whether somebody was killed or lost their life in another manner, whether that person was killed in combat, and so on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, as I said earlier, didn't study the specific causes of death or going missing of the individuals included in our list, but we did cross-reference the records of missing persons with the records of DNA identifications for the human remains of persons that were exhumed from mass graves and other graves in the region of Srebrenica and broader area of Srebrenica in Eastern Bosnia. By doing this, we, first of all, want to provide a proof of death of these individuals. Having a record of DNA identification is far more than having a record of a person reported missing. So DNA identifications confirm the death of these individuals. Further, they confirm much more than just the death. It is that they confirm these persons were not buried in regular graves in cemeteries; these persons were exhumed from graves, unmarked graves, hidden graves in the area of Srebrenica. That most certainly tells something about circumstances which we don't discuss in the report. It is not our task to discuss the circumstances of making the graves and killing the people in events related to these graves. We don't have the expertise and we don't have sources to do so. I believe our report should be read as a background report that is discussing the scale of victimisation of the fall of Srebrenica. Moreover, it provides proof of death for a large number of victims. As of 2009, 66 per cent, as far as I remember, of the missing persons have been confirmed as DNA-identified cases, so these are no more missing persons. These are people who are dead. Of whom we know they are buried in mass graves and other graves in the Srebrenica region. Further, we have if our reports statistics that show that 80 per cent of the people identified so far, 80 per cent, approximately, were found in the mass graves that are known as ICTY mass graves. These ICTY mass graves is a separate category of graves in which ICTY conducted the investigation, and there is -- there exists additional evidence in relation to these particular sites. So we provide evidence that is telling 66 per cent of the missing have been confirmed as dead as of now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, it was a rather lengthy --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- answer to a compound question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please focus a little bit more on the specific question put to you. And we should have back on the screen page 4 in both languages of this document. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I asked you to carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have any conceptual differences with Mr. Brunborg during the work on this project? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that we would have differences of serious nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1776 shown in e-court, which is the 2009 report, page 38. In the Serbian language, could we please look at Annex 2 of your report titled, "Definitions of Terms in Relation to the Srebrenica Victims."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see it. My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: English page in e-court is 34. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now your question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this report of yours it is clear that you use the term of a missing person by defining it through the date or place of disappearance, that is to say, when the person was seen alive for the last time. So you were not necessarily interested in when the person may have been killed. You say here this can be either the date when the person submitting information saw the person alive for the last time or it can be based on the information provided by an eye-witness. My question is this: What method did you use to ascertain whether a person was also a witness or whether that person received such information from another witness?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about missing, date and place of missing or last seen, was obtained by the ICRC. This is not that we collected it from informants or sources; it is the ICRC collected it from their informants. And they accepted people very selectively based on strict criteria. It would have to be the family members on the first place or people somehow related to the victims from whom the reports were accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your answer, is such a report reliable, given the fact that it was treated in two different ways?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it treated in two different ways. But generally I find the ICRC list of missing persons very reliable. And in addition to this, there is another source, an independent source, on the missing persons that would be the ICMP, the International Commission for Missing Persons, the one who provided the DNA identification of the victims. They too collected information on the missing persons during the process of collection of blood samples for the DNA analysis, so they contacted the families or families contacted them, and based on this they have their own list of missing persons from Srebrenica. As we see, the two match each other very well. So the records of ICRC are found in large numbers in ICMP records and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, tell me this, please: Are their lists reliable in terms of the dates of disappearance? I have in mind the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: ICMP, as a matter of fact, does not report exact dates of disappearance. They use, for all victims, one date, the 11th of July, to describe the fact that these are Srebrenica-identified persons. Only ICRC provides the specific dates. How reliable it is? It is as reliable as the reports of the informants of ICRC and their knowledge of the disappearance. This is just what people remember and what they think happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Both of these organisations you referred to, the ICRC and the ICMP, are they NGOs?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes, these are. ICRC is an international organisation. Whether I could say it is an NGO, I wouldn't know, really, as a matter of fact. It is a humanitarian organisation with a long history of providing humanitarian support to the victims of any conflict. And ICMP is also an international organisation with a specific mandate to provide DNA identifications of the victims of the war in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know all that. But I just wanted to ask you whether they are non-governmental organisations or not. If they are governmental organisations, perhaps you can tell us what government they are part of.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not part of any government. They are supported by donations from various countries. So in the sense -- in this sense they are just operating independently and not for a given government. They represent the international community in their actions and fulfill the mandates that were made for them at some points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand your answer and I'll move on to the next question. Is what NGOs have more reliable than the data procured by the armed forces directly participating in some hostilities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a question that I cannot really answer. Well, I guess you are referring to the ICRC lists and ICMP lists of missing or identified persons versus the lists provided by the army, so it is -- I really can't say what is more reliable. I do definitely trust very much the lists provided by ICRC and ICMP. And why? Because I know the method how they operate, what kind of approach they use to collect the information, to process it, and I work -- they work up to the international standards. On the other hand you are telling me what do I think about the military records. I believe they must be reliable too. They are issued by state authorities. Moreover, the state authorities issued these records for an important purpose, for postmortem benefits to the families of the fallen soldiers and other people on these lists. So they must be reliable too. So that is -- yeah, there is -- I can't say I trust this more or that. I trust both and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You could have provided a shorter answer in response to my question. And I wanted to ask you to do that for my next question. Why did you then change the entries of the armed forces and not the data provided by the NGOs?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
