utterances.text: I didn't change anything in the lists that were made for the 2009 report because the additional information obtained from the Ministry of Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina supported the fact of including certain individuals among Srebrenica missing. So there was no need to make any changes. The thing is that even the best source might be containing inconsistencies and problems. It is not so that statistical sources are perfect. And my role as a statistician is to check the quality of each source I use for my work. And if I identify inconsistencies or records that need to be removed, I have to do that. Why? Because it is a sort of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't ask you that. I asked you why you changed the request to the Bosnian government. In any case, I'll take your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your question was: "Why did you then change the entries of the armed forces and not the data provided by the NGOs?" That was your question. And not why you changed the request to the Bosnian government. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Also with respect to the last question that he asks, that effectively misstates the evidence in the case. There was no change to any request that was made to the Bosnian authorities, the army, the Ministry of Defence, or anything like that. There's no evidence of that in the record. So either it's a misinterpretation or I would ask General Tolimir to restate his question in a manner that's consistent with the evidence that's been provided by this witness and not in a misleading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since I don't have time to go back to some details where the witness can explain her work, I will put the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you put the lists of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the lists provided by the ICRC or not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use the lists of the army to compile the list of Srebrenica missing or identified persons. I did not use these records at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will see that a bit later. I would like to ask something about the third and fifth paragraph of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 81 in the Serbian language and 77 in the English, it is the 2009 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it, I will put my question. A moment ago you said that the information about the circumstances of disappearance was collected by the ICRC by the next of kin. And in the next paragraph, when addressing the issue of the lists, you said that the lists of the ICRC of the Srebrenica missing and the lists of the ICMP provide certain differences in interpretation about certain elements of the Srebrenica missing and that you see no reason to exclude either. When I asked you about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tolimir please repeat his last question. It wasn't intelligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were asked by the interpreters to repeat the last part of your question. I will assist you. Your last sentence ended with "and that you see no reason to exclude either." And then, "When I asked you about --" The interpreters didn't catch the last part. Please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What differences do you have in mind in paragraph 5 in relation to the elements provided for the Srebrenica missing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring to the paragraph 5 that we have on the screen; right? Which begins, "Also 1998 records were included ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. The penultimate line in quotation, it reads: "Srebrenica related."

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It is so that this paragraph is about 1998 records that were not reported in the latest list of October 2008 of Srebrenica missing provided to us by ICRC. These 1998 records come from the overall lists of missing persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, entire country, also made by the ICRC. These 1998 records were selected from this overall country-wide list according to our criteria of a Srebrenica missing person. These criteria are discussed in this report in Annex 2. So the Srebrenica-related person can be understand, first of all, as a person who satisfies -- or a record of whom satisfies our criteria of being a Srebrenica missing person in terms of area and time as specified in Annex 2. On the other hand, there is this separate list of October 2008 by ICRC who listed their Srebrenica missing persons. So we see no contradiction between these two. It is that in -- according our criteria additional 1998 records should be included, additional to the October 2008 ICRC Srebrenica missing persons list. There is no contradiction. We include them. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, the first line of that paragraph, if you would have a look on it. There we can see the OTP list but were not listed on the IRCR Srebrenica 2008 update. Is that -- what is "IRCR" or is it a typo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It isn't a typo. Perhaps I could help understand, better understand, this issue. If I would make a drawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you just say what does it mean, IRCR. What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the ICRC is the organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking for IRCR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, that is a typo, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is a typo. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why did you state in the report that you don't know what criteria was used by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is because I don't exactly know what criteria they used for their list. Perhaps they used the reports of the informants of the families who told them these persons went missing in the context of the fall of Srebrenica. We, on the other hand, used two formal criteria, the area and time, for compiling our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a possibility then that the ICRC puts a limit on what makes it on to the list because they did not provide any reference of the criteria? Then if we understand it that way, any person whose DNA was analysed could make it on to the list.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know the rationale behind the ICRC list of Srebrenica missing and I don't want to speculate. But as a matter of fact, it is a fact that several Srebrenica missing persons lists exist. There is one list here, there is the list of ICRC, there is the list of ICMP, that the Bosnian Commission for Tracing Missing Persons will have their own list, now the Missing Persons Institute in Bosnia and Herzegovina will have their own list, and it is not so that there is one-to-one correspondence between all these lists. There will be slight differences in the number of reported persons by every source. But there will be a core which is common as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain why in the Srebrenica-related lists of missing you included those who went missing and were last seen alive in Baljkovica, which is the place where the column left the RS and entered the federation territory, which is not in the Srebrenica area at all?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Baljkovica, as far as I remember, is part of the municipality of Zvornik, I think. And as such it is part of the formal criterion of the Srebrenica area used in our report. This is why it is listed. And relating -- in relation to the events in Baljkovica, it is not our role to study the military or historical background of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since that was not your role, are you presenting a case in your report which would reflect what indeed happened or does your report serve a different purpose?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, it is a background report on the victimisation of the fall of Srebrenica and patterns of victimisation of the fall. By saying "patterns," I also mean a territorial pattern. It is so that places of disappearance are included in this report, particular, specific places, and also places as municipalities. Any statistic can be provided for any given place. If this report is read together with other reports like military narrative or a historical background report, it is possible to make adjustments according to what is believed is needed, simply. But as a matter of fact, I think the context -- the definitions used in this report are appropriate, I believe, of the area and times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you included it all in the general formulation about Srebrenica, can you tell us whether you studied the statements made by OTP witnesses before this Court and the data they provided on the place and date of death and the circumstances thereof?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't study the witness statements before this Court. And I -- because it is not part of my task to do so and was not needed for making this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the Court then be deceived as to the place and time of those events? Let's use an example. Mr. Ruez was an investigator of this Tribunal and he appeared as a witness. He asserts before the Court that he saw 600 corpses in Bare. It is in D166, page 595 of the transcript in the Krstic case. My question is this: If it is irrelevant to you what the witnesses said and the only important thing for you is what you have to say, do we then need to have anyone testifying about those events at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this was a misstatement of the last answer of the witness. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe it also does not properly reflect the statement of Mr. Ruez. And in that sense it's misleading to the witness. And I think it's likely to elicit an inappropriate response, and that's the reason why I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have that document on the screen. D166, if that is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The correct number is D166, page 595 [Realtime transcript read in error "559"] in the Krstic transcript. The Finnish pathologist did the work. And I gave the reference pertaining to this testimony so as to avoid putting up on the screen D166.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question is: Did she take into account information received from the pathologist defining the place, date, and manner of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously pathological reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the right page on the screen. We would like to have the right page on the screen and an indication -- you said it's page 559. On the screen we have 589.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 595. I apologise. 595. Maybe I made the mistake. I'm sorry. We need 595.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And can you give us the line on that page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 8 to 17 in Serbian. And the same goes for the English language. It's a whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you take into account the reports compiled by pathologists and other experts who worked to find the circumstances of death of the victims in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For our report we didn't use these reports. No pathological reports used for our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does your Demographic Unit analyse all sources that could have some relevant information about the place, date, or manner of death? And does it also analyse testimony of the witnesses who appear in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be an impossible task to analyse all the sources and all the testimonies. It is not feasible, simply. Well, we plan our reports according to what we think is the most appropriate and feasible, and we try to restrict ourselves in our work. We have certain goals we want to reach, and we select sources that allow us to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So here we can see two sources: One source are the Finnish pathologists; the other is Jean Ruez, the witness. And we also have another report referencing 600 victims. Another witness talks about 500 victims. So these differences are something that should be take into account. Or do you think that for the purposes of your research it is a negligible difference?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first of all think that aggregate statistics, 500, 600, 3.000, 10.000, are completely meaningless for this kind of work we have presented in our report. We require that personal details of a victim are available. We make lists of victims. So these kind of general statements with overall statistics cannot be simply used in this type of work we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that your report is a global report about the events in Srebrenica because it includes everything related to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it includes everything related to Srebrenica. It does include records of missing persons related to the fall of Srebrenica. And in the report it is defined what is understood by a Srebrenica missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Here is an example. In Exhibit 151, PW-016, a protected witness, said that at a certain location he saw several hundreds of dead, or another 150; and then near a cemetery, 30; and then at a fourth location, 25 to 30. So we see that here a single witness mentions more than 500 dead. Is this a relevant information that should have been made available to you because it speaks about the precise place, date, and manner of death?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you said Exhibit 151. Is it a P or a D Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I believe this should be Defence Exhibit D151 and should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I quoted it from page 2, paragraph 3, lines 14, 23, and 28. I made a wrong reference and now we have a wrong document, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here in the third paragraph it says, in line 7, there were more than 300 dead. That's what he says. More than 300 dead and a significant number of wounded. Which means that the total number of victims could even be higher. And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help me. Where is it in this document? You say --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the third paragraph, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then we have P1174, page 2, line 14, 23, and 28, where the witness speaks about the same event but then says that at another place there was 25 people; at another, 30 people; 150 at the fourth place. So are these data relevant for your Demographic Unit which is engaged in finding out the place, the date, and the manner of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But these numbers are not associated with lists of names. There are no personal details of victims available from these kind of statements. So for my work these statements cannot be used. It is not the approach that we have taken. We work with concrete people, with names and other information about these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a pity that we haven't seen P1174 page 2 that I referenced, lines 14, 23, and 28, so that I can ask my following question. But then let me put it this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tolimir. You should just ask for this document. You haven't done that. You just mentioned it. Wait, it will come up on the screen, and you may put a question in relation to that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document P1174 should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All right. Now we have the document. Can we have page 2. Of course, do not broadcast it outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This witness describes the exact route of the column from Srebrenica to Baljkovica and says where the victims were left. And then at page 2, line 40, you can see it on the right-hand side of the screen, number 25 to 30. Then line 23, the last number in that line, 30 and a little dash after that. Then line 28, close to the date 13/7/1995, deaths, where he mentions 150 dead and seriously wounded civilians, and so and so forth. So this witness gives an accurate description of what he saw on the way to Konjevic Polje. Are those data relevant for the investigators engaged in finding the place, the date, and the manner of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the investigators, these data might be relevant, but this is not my work. It is a different approach that we have taken than studying the information from witness statements. I can imagine that a study of witness statements can be put together, absolutely. Why not? But this is not what I have done. It's a different approach totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with you that they are different approaches; however, is this approach a more precise approach containing more information about the place, the date, and the manner of death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not because the names of victims are not there. So it is more precise in relation to the timing and location of certain incidents, but it doesn't give precise information about victimisation of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't give those data to you, but it does give data about the date, place, and manner of death of certain persons, and you talk about those same things in your reports, so aren't those data here more precise? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think you have got the answer this witness can provide you with. She told you her way to compile lists and to deal with certain information. You got the answer already. I understand your position, but you shouldn't continue asking the same question. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we now have P07170 -- P1776, page 104 in Serbian, 94 in English. Let me repeat, P1776. In Serbian 104, in English 97. I need that in order to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we zoom in. And rotate the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So here we can see that in this table you determined the date of death based on information provided by the BiH army and the lists of the OTP, and this is exactly the case that you spoke about earlier, the case of 220 people who came from the OTP list from 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And here we can see that this list -- that this list also contains the DNA data and that in order to harmonise the DNA data and the BiH data, you sent that request for assistance to the defence ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And my question is: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber this table and can you explain how can it happen that in the mass graves and on the lists made by the OTP we can find persons who died in 1994, 1993, and 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first of all want to explain that DoD, this is the symbol used in this table to describe the date of disappearance or death in a few cases, shouldn't be read as the details about the dead. The military response was also referring to the going missing of the same persons. So it is not that we still -- that we do have information about the dead and place of death. We still have to deal with disappearance date and place. This is first. Second, there are certain dates, DoD military, that are reported as 1992, 1994, 1993. These are the initial reports of the militaries that were clarified and corrected to 1995. It happens, as I said yesterday, that these kind of registers are dynamic systems, and it happens that these systems are often not updated for a very long time. So the information entered at some point remains there for a very long time uncorrected. Obviously, to more recent -- according to more recent knowledge, it is possible to -- for certain cases to provide information that is different than that in the system. So that explains the difference in the reported dates of disappearance. And further, there is no surprise that for several persons on these lists -- on this list also the ICMP information about the DNA identification is available. After all, this is a sample of -- or subsample of the Srebrenica missing persons whom we systematically cross-reference with the DNA identifications. So what we see in the entire list, that would be the 66 per cent of identifications, must be also resembled in these kind of little subsamples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, does this table maybe tell us that there were cases of false registration of missing persons or some other deficiencies related to the DNA analysis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say a false registration of missing persons. And I wouldn't speak of deficiencies related to DNA analysis. What I'm saying, it can happen in chaotic circumstances of war that systems registering certain events are imperfect, and that is an example of such a system. At some point a person could have been reported missing as of, I don't know, April 1992. Later obviously the person reappeared to go missing again perhaps in 1995. This is a theory, I cannot -- I cannot say I have a proof for this theory for every single case on this list, but these things happen. This is a war situation we are speaking about, and in war situations statistical reporting or military reporting are imperfect, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us which information can be considered more complete: Information coming from NGOs 14 years after the fact or information coming from military institutions and state organs who had a certain legal obligation vis-à-vis the families of the deceased? What is more precise?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think your question is very imprecise. I think you are referring, by NGOs 14 years after the war, or the fact, as you say, to the reports by ICRC and their missing persons records, and I think that these reports are reliable most definitely. It is not that ICRC started making their list 14 years after the war. They started operating during the war already and have continued up till the present day to make the lists as good as possible. And whether the military system is better than that, it should be equally good at least, right? It is not that I'm saying that military records are better because it is just a military system. It is a matter of how the system has been maintained over the years and what kind of improvements have been brought to the system, whether there were subsequent updates or there were no updates, et cetera, et cetera. So it is not that I can give a full -- yeah, my full opinion about these kind of issues in the case of military lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind that this is information relevant for judicial organs, I mean here various consequences arising from the death and from death registers, can you tell us why was it that the BiH army did not accept to harmonise their lists with the ICRC lists? And I call ICRC here an NGO.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you are saying the BiH army did not accept to harmonise. Has anybody asked for this? I don't think so. It is just that these two organisations have operated parallel, I think. ICRC doing their work and the army doing their records. And whether there was an exchange of information between them and why should it be, I don't really know. I'm not studying these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The person who compiled this list testified here, Mr. Brunborg, and he said that the BiH army in certain cases did not agree to change the data on place of death and manner of death. Do you have any information on this? Can you tell us something? It was him, Mr. Brunborg, who told us that you have more detailed information on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you give us a reference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. While we hear the answer, my assistant is going to try to find the exact reference. I remember very well that Brunborg said that the army would not harmonise certain number of entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe it will be of assistance to Mr. Gajic and also General Tolimir, I think the reference that he's making is to transcript page 10112. And that is during the course of Dr. Brunborg's testimony. And perhaps we'll have to look from line 6 all the way through to line 23. And if we can get that up on the screen, maybe Mr. Gajic can confirm or General Tolimir can confirm that that's the right reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. He questioned -- he led the questioning of Mr. Brunborg here, so I certainly trust him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did can you tell us, do you know how many cases were there when the BiH army did not accept to change their list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you first that I doubt seriously that Mr. Brunborg has a specific knowledge what the army did what their records, how many they accepted or rejected, whatever. What we know is the response that was provided to us by the military authority. I think you also received a copy of this response. It was discussed earlier today. And in the response there is a remark that the authorities were unable to provide the information for I think seven individuals of the 142 for whom information was requested. I'm now checking the actual response. Yes, it is correct. They were unable for seven persons to find copies of appropriate documents. That's all we know. And that's all we have in terms of documents or, rather, lack of documents. And whether the army corrected their records is a totally completely separate thing. It is not of what something that we are aware of or asked for. So we asked for information, we were provided with information, and whether the army subsequently made any changes in their register, it is beyond our knowledge and we cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have enough time to discuss this at length. And since I discussed it with Mr. Brunborg, it is all right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court pages 44 and 40. In Serbian 44 and in English 40. It's table number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document we have on the screen; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, once again, P1776.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see table 3/1, cases from the 2008 ICRC Srebrenica list by category. And then we have the categories here and the numbers of cases. So we see that the ICRC confirmed the death of 3.459 persons. In relation to that, I want to know the following: What were the criteria employed by the ICRC in order to denote a certain person as missing or dead in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, of course, don't know exactly. It is, again, the ICRC who decided when to close their cases. I'm aware of an exchange of information between ICRC and ICMP with respect to identifications, DNA identifications, of missing persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I can safely say these type of reports must have been part of closing their cases. It is also so that there is -- there exists an ICRC Working Group on missing persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As part of this group, ICRC co-operates with the Bosnian Commission for Tracing Missing Persons. It is the commission that is involved in exhumations and in collecting all kinds of reports issued about the victims from exhumations, including the final death certificates signed by the court pathologists that are used in declaring missing persons dead. I can imagine, again, that ICRC uses this kind of information in declaring missing persons as dead and closing the cases. There won't be, of course, again, a one-to-one association between the identifications that are available at ICMP or the federal or state Commission for Tracing Missing Persons because information is sent with certain delays and received with delays and then there is time needed to update the databases, et cetera, et cetera. So there will be differences in the numbers of these closed cases of dead people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have our second break now. We adjourn, and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before the break we called up document P1 -- it was page 44 anyway of that document, and table 3.1. Could we please return to that now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think that is document P1776.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1776.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Everybody in the courtroom wanted to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting, I'll ask my question. The ICRC established the death of 3459 persons, we'll see that figure in the table, and they say that these deaths are connected with Srebrenica. And you in your report state that there are 5061 [Realtime transcript read in error "561"] persons whose identity was allegedly established. How do you account for this difference between 3459 and 5061? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. May I please have the document in the e-court because my e-court is not showing me anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that there is a technical problem at the moment. It's not possible to bring that document up. The Registry is working on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I think I still have answer the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number Mr. Tolimir mentioned from page 40 English version of the report was 3.459 of closed cases dead persons reported by ICRC in October 2008. And the second number was 5.061 persons. This number can be for instance found in table 1 in the report which is on page 6. This is the number of DNA identifications issued by the ICMP and confirmed in the record of OTP Srebrenica missing persons. So the ICMP number confirmed in OTP list is much higher than the number of ICRC closed cases dead. And I think I already explained the difference when I was speaking before the break about how ICRC most likely closes their cases. I mentioned that information is forwarded from ICMP and other organisations involved in the identification of the victims to ICRC, and there are certain delays and there are certain time-periods required to process information at ICRC and so this explains perhaps a part of the difference. There are possibly other factors which I'm unaware of, so again it is hard for me to say why there is no one-to-one correspondence between these two totals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have the table on the screen in both languages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what you're saying, that you don't know, can you answer the following question: Does the OTP mostly rely on the information received from the ICMP and only respects their lists while neglecting the lists made by other participants? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We mostly rely on the information from the ICMP. It doesn't mean we neglect information from other relevant sources on identification of victims. But why we consider the ICMP identifications the most important, it is largely because of the method itself. It is the DNA matching and -- first profiling and matching. ICMP does that very professionally. They follow certain standard operating procedures and are recognised as important and a reliable organisation in their area. Secondly, there is in Bosnia and Herzegovina a law on missing persons that was introduced around the year of 2005 or 2006. I don't recall exactly. This law says that missing persons, every missing person in this country needs to be identified by using the DNA method, so the simply existence of this law makes it really necessary before a person can be declared dead to be first identified by the DNA identification. So that are the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the reason why later on, on the lists there are persons who died after the war, on the lists of persons whose DNA was analysed, as well of persons -- as well as persons who died before the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what lists you are referring as the fact of issuing a DNA identification. Does it mean automatically that date of death and place of death and circumstances of death are identified as well? In many instances, yes, but not for every missing person. So if there are inconsistent cases of persons who were reported missing before the fall of Srebrenica and after the fall of Srebrenica, say, in 1996 and later, I think these cases basically do not confirm to our criteria of including records of missing persons in our OTP of Srebrenica missing, so these persons are not part of our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We've seen that Mr. Brunborg wrote that first paragraph in that 65 ter 1708 document and he states the minimum number of victims killed by the VRS immediately after the fall of the enclave. He says that was his task. But what would be the maximum number of victims that can be established by these methods? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what Mr. Brunborg did in his article is his responsibility, of course. What would be the maximum number? Well, what would be the maximum number of missing persons related to the fall of Srebrenica? I personally haven't estimated such a number. I think it would be possible. There are statistical methods that allow this kind of estimation. A certain estimate was produced by ICMP, by Tom Parsons, the forensic director of the ICMP, who estimated, who made a point estimate of missing persons related to the fall of Srebrenica and provided a confidence interval which would, with a high confidence, 95 per cent confidence, contain this point estimate, but it is not necessarily the maximum number. There are other statistical methods based on capped or recapped [phoen] approach that would allow to make such an estimate. I wouldn't have a ready answer for this. If any is sought, then I can think about producing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For us to be able to see what you're talking about, I would like to show page 46 in Serbian and page 42 in English. And that's a section that deals with the ICMP and DNA analyses. While we're waiting, I'll ask you the following: Does that list of the ICMP and does the maximum number of DNA analyses performed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the end of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were asked again to repeat the last part of your question. The last sentence we have on the screen is: "Does this list of the ICMP and does the maximum number of the DNA analyses performed --" and then the recording stopped. Please repeat the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked whether that list and the number of DNA analyses performed, the maximum number that the Demographic Unit has to assume working for the needs of this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never had a particular number in mind when trying to make these lists of Srebrenica missing and identified persons. It is rather an approach that should be seen as a reconstruction of the demographic reality of this episode of war. So reconstruction means making a list of people for whom there are good reasons to believe they are the victims associated with the fall of Srebrenica. And making a number beforehand, without having such a list, does not make much sense at all. So no target number on our side on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph 2 of the document we have on our screens. And it says, the first sentence: "A concise yet exhaustive overview of the exhumation and identification status in the former Yugoslavia, and in Srebrenica in particular, is not available from a single organisation." And you go on to say, toward the end of this paragraph: "Unfortunately, this database does not yet exist in a useable electronic format." Bearing in mind all you have said or all you say here, did you consider the possibility that somebody has that information but they are -- have not been forwarded to all parties in electronic format to be harmonised? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in the report, the information about missing persons is scattered across several organisations. Attempts have been made to integrate the various lists circulated around and to make one central database. Recently I hear that the missing persons institute in Bosnia and Herzegovina achieved their first result in this area. There were media reports that this institute have made a list of all missing persons from the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Srebrenica would be, of course, part of this database. It is a relatively large list of 35.000 persons that was reported -- approximately 35.000 persons reported for the entire war and entire country of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This list is longer, obviously, than the ICRC list of missing persons from Bosnia which has approximately 22.000 cases. I -- it is a very recent development. I have not contacted the missing persons institute with a question for a list of missing persons related to the fall of Srebrenica. Perhaps they have such a list. I don't know, simply. So it would be a possibility to take a look at what they have. But as a matter of fact, my feeling is that we have enough information based on the ICRC records to -- to make a list of missing persons related to the fall of Srebrenica. It is a reliable source with a relatively detailed reporting of the victims, and it is certainly a very good basis for making an initial list of missing persons. So I wouldn't be seeing any point in going and asking for new records on missing persons. What matters most at this stage are the records of identified persons, DNA identifications issued by the ICMP. And this is available, we have it all. Any record issued and relevant to Srebrenica is at the OTP. New updates are sent systematically every six months. That is the material that is most essential for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have gotten to the question I'm interested in. Who has the monopoly over information about which Mr. Tokaca spoke and documented, D38, paragraph 3? Could you tell us who that is and whether the ICRC harmonise this database as the main protagonist? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the D38, paragraph 3, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be called up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's Exhibit D38, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting, please tell us whether the ICRC will be in charge of this unified database and whether these data will be of a limiting nature and binding for everybody? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like you to explain what is this unified database. Is this a database of missing persons institute I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I take it that -- oh, interesting. In your list of exhibits there is an entry that the translation is pending. Now I see there is a translation already. That's fine. Which paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Paragraph 3. Where it says: "The biggest problem in B&H is perfidious monopoly on information."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is why I asked whether the ICRC will play a dominant role in the creation of the electronic database, the harmonised electronic database. I believe the witness wanted to know what database I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is not the database of Mirsad Tokaca we are talking here but the database of missing persons that is being created or has been created recently by the missing persons institute. That is my understanding. And with this understanding I'm answering this question. The missing persons institute is a body that involves all ethnicities, all ethnic groups, major ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and ICRC will be slowly handing over their records to this institute. This institute is meant to become a leading organisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina with the mandate to keep records of the missing and subsequently the records on the identification of the missing persons. From what I know from media reports is that it is not ICRC but ICMP that very actively supported the idea of creation of this institute and already helped the institute in their work, in particular in creation of this large database with 35.000 missing persons from Bosnia. So it is not -- it is so that ICRC will be handing over material to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Time will tell whether your answer or my question is correct. The paragraph just below the paragraph begins with: "The biggest problem in B&H is a perfidious monopoly on information, Tokaca said, pointing out that the IDC wanted to break this monopoly by compiling the Bosnian crime atlas." My question is this: If such information was provided by the director of the IDC in Sarajevo Mr. Tokaca, what does it tell us about the context of the attempts so far to establish the number of missing and killed in Srebrenica in order to harmonise it? What does it tell you as a demographer?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that Mr. Tokaca makes his statements. And I have nothing do with his statements, and I don't live in Bosnia, and I don't know the realities in Bosnia; so I don't know what kind of monopoly he meant. But as a matter of fact, it wasn't easy to harmonise the integration of these various databases. It took quite a long time, long time after the war ended, to finally have one database on missing persons in Bosnia. So -- but there is such a database. It exists. That means it was possible in the end, which is a good sign. So if there was any monopoly, of which I am unaware, so obviously now it has been gone because things are going in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. He is probably more familiar with it than either you or me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down the page to see what else he has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He says that "70 people were buried at the Potocari Memorial Centre who did not perish in the area of Srebrenica." Can you see that? It is the penultimate paragraph. Can you tell us how it was possible and whether there were any manipulations with the lists and the way they were created?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the 70 people buried in Potocari Memorial Centre. And I want to note it is just a press report who is allegedly quoting Mr. Tokaca, but this is just a press report, media report. What Tokaca said is perhaps this or something else. Well, in my work I don't use the records from Potocari from the Memorial Centre, so from this point of view this information is of no relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be relevant to know that the same thing was confirmed by Researcher Ivanisevic in the report that was forwarded by the Defence? It was used -- it was used by the Defence in a quote from that book.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, sir, if I tell you that it is possible, perhaps it is possible, perhaps not, but I don't think that Mr. Ivanisevic is a good reference for our discussion here. Why? Because his number of Srebrenica victim is not 7.000 to 8.000, it is 700 to 800, so he is seeing the whole problem in a totally completely different perspective. And what happened in Potocari, who is buried there, is the responsibility of the local authorities who are in charge of the Potocari Memorial Centre. And I think these kind of issues should be addressed to these people. And I don't think it makes sense to address these issues here in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you now moved to another topic and we are short of time, you seem to be discussing something else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have page 26 in the Serbian language and page 22 in the English of the 2009 report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I didn't understand your last comment, because the witness was exactly addressing you in relation to your question. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps in her report we will come across a different answer. Could we please have Ms. Tabeau's report. Page 26 in Serbian, 22 in the English version, the penultimate paragraph which reads as follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is again P1776.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this part of the report, there's a mention of the number of inhabitants of Srebrenica. I quote: "It is presumed that in Srebrenica before it fell there were some 40.000 people. However, no exact figure is known. The lack of data on the exact population at risk makes it difficult to calculate the proper mortality rates, so we had to choose another methodology, i.e., ratios or proportions of death." I want to ask you this: What other criteria did you use when putting forth information about the assessed number of people in Srebrenica before it fell, the number being 40.000?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the report says that the actual number of the Srebrenica living -- of the population living in Srebrenica at the time of fall is unknown. This is what I read on my page. Twenty-two in this paragraph. The 40.000 is one of the guesses, probably informed guesses, circulated widely by various organisations. In the town of Srebrenica there were initially, 1991, many less people. It was a small town of approximately 6.000 people. And, yes, it is believed the size increased considerably, depending on the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So as not to waste all of our time on this question, since your answer is rather broad, could you please tell us whether you relied on any Srebrenica municipal documents, or did you rely on some other sources? And perhaps you can say yes or no, either you did or you didn't.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did rely on the information from the 1991 population census, that is, the population size at the outbreak of the conflict. And no other sources were used, as no other sources were reliable enough to make a judgement or assessment or estimate of the population size of those living in the Srebrenica area by mid-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have D177 next, please. Sorry, D117. It is a document from the municipality of Srebrenica which kept statistics about the population living in Srebrenica before the events in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it now. Can you tell us this, please: Have you had previous occasion to see this document?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I didn't see this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what is before you, can you see that we have the exact figures of the population per municipality that were within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, perhaps it's enough to have the English version on the screen, then the witness would be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's very small. Now it's better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there precise information on the population within the enclave before the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the population reported in the 1991 census - this is what I said - before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: However, this breakdown dates back to July 1995, that is to say, the time of the events. You can see the date. It's the 11th of January, 1995. It is in the heading.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, but what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was whether you had precise information on the number of the population in 1995 during this period?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the information that was required to calculate the mortality ratios. All the analyses presented in our report in section 2.5 are done by ethnicity. These overall totals available here for January 1995 is -- don't include the information about ethnic groups. They don't show the age and sex breakdown of the population. These are very general figures, and from this point of view these figures are useless for the analysis that we were planning to do. And the methodology we applied was based on the 1991 population census but it is not unusual in demography to calculate probabilities of death. Probabilities of death are always calculated in relation to the population size at the beginning of the period concerned. In this case, it would be the period of war and, in particular, the events in 1995 as related to the initial size of the population in 1991. Methodologically it is a sound approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be better to use a list from 1995 or to use this register of the municipal bodies dating from January 1994? From a demographic point of view, which would be more appropriate?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not January 1994. It is January 1995. This is the date on the document. And as I said, these are rough figures that do not show the necessary breakdown of the population by ethnicity, by age, and by sex. This is what we needed for our analysis, and this is what is not available here. Secondly, this list here, these statistics here, cannot be linked at individual level to the victims that we collected for the Srebrenica -- for the fall of Srebrenica. So what I'm trying to say, these overall statistics, that are approximations most certainly, can no way be associated with the exact numbers that we have from our victims lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will decide whether these are precise or approximate numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's not -- no more time to move to another document. We have reached the end of today's hearing and have to adjourn. And you may continue at an appropriate time next week or the week after. I've heard that on Monday there's another witness scheduled, and this witness, Ms. Tabeau, will be available at any time because she's working in this building. What is the situation, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You are correct, Mr. President. We do have another witness, and Dr. Tabeau will be available. I'd just like to get a sense from General Tolimir how much further cross-examination he might have for her at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that possible to indicate, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe we will conclude within the announced time. I will only ask Mrs. Tabeau to respond directly to my questions, to proceed in a more efficient manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was the case. We have to adjourn for today and resume next Monday, 2.15, in Courtroom II, because this courtroom is needed for another trial. Thank you very much. I have to remind you again not to communicate with either party during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I do recall that Dr. Tabeau made a reference to a project that she was working on concerning the 58 names indicated by Mr. Ivanisevic. I don't believe that any communication is required for that purpose. But to the extent there might be incidental communication, just in terms of logistics, sort of providing the information as the office receives it, I suppose I should bring that to your attention that that's a probability. If the material arrives to the Office of the Prosecutor and not to Dr. Tabeau directly, there will have to be some contact in order to provide her with those records. And with your leave I'd like to be able to do that, but I think it's important to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there can't be a problem, also not for the Defence, to forward material which can help both parties during the cross and re-examination of this witness. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness works for the OTP, she works in this building, and it would be too much to ask not to even say hello to her colleagues. Therefore we have no such expectation of this witness. There should be no difference to the measures applied save for the fact that this witness works for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Of course the normal contact of her colleagues is permitted, but no discussion about the content of her testimony we will receive at a later time in this trial. Thank you very much. We adjourn. And I was told that we are not sitting in Courtroom II on Monday but in Courtroom I on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
